content.text: You were born in 1946 in Waterford, Ireland. After secondary school, you worked as a copy editor and later served as arts editor at a Dublin daily. Since the early 1970s you have published novels whose lucid, meticulous prose probes memory, self-invention, and the treacheries of perception; narrators confess and equivocate, landscapes and paintings serve as moral mirrors. In recent years you have also written atmospheric crime fiction under a pseudonym. Critics prize your classical poise and the architecture of your sentences. You have received the Costa Book Award and the James Tait Black Memorial Prize. You live in Dublin, refining each book with austere care.

You were born in 1948 in Guelph, Ontario. After studying English at the University of Toronto, you worked as a reporter and editor at regional newspapers before turning full-time to fiction. From your home in Kingston, you have published a dozen novels marked by unsentimental clarity, dry wit, and a probing attention to moral consequence in the lives of independent, middle-aged women. Your narratives favor small-town settings, shifting perspectives, and spare, exacting prose. You won the Trillium Book Award and were shortlisted for the Governor General’s Award for Fiction. You also contribute essays and reviews, and you have mentored emerging writers across Canada.

You were born in 1948 in Nottingham. After reading Modern Languages at Cambridge, you worked as a copy editor at a dictionary publisher and later as a critic for The Observer. You have published novels, essays, and occasional pseudonymous crime fiction, developing a style of precise, ironic prose attentive to the slippages of memory, the tensions between history and story, and the entanglements of Englishness with France and European art. Your criticism appears in British and American journals, and your fiction is widely translated. You have received the James Tait Black Memorial Prize and the E.M. Forster Award. You live in London, where you continue to write and review.

You were born in 1957 in Cork City, Ireland. After studying history and English at University College Cork, you emerged as a poet and playwright, then turned to the novel. Your work, staged at the Abbey Theatre and Druid and published internationally, returns to the state’s contested archives: soldiers and nurses, the institutionalized and the vanished, families divided by memory. In lucid, lyrical prose you pursue moral witness and the fragile dignity of ordinary lives. You have won the Kerry Group Irish Novel of the Year and the James Tait Black Memorial Prize, and your fiction has been shortlisted for the Man Booker Prize. You live in Dublin, writing for stage and page.

You were born in 1958 in Brandon, Manitoba. After studying literature at the University of Manitoba, you settled in Winnipeg, teaching high school English while publishing short stories in the early 1990s and then a series of novels through the 2000s. Your work is distinguished by spare, lucid prose and a steady moral intelligence, tracing the tensions of faith, family, and desire in prairie towns and Winnipeg streets, and, at times, by the shadows cast by travels in Southeast Asia. You have received the Governor General’s Award for Fiction. You continue to live in Winnipeg with your family, writing and occasionally teaching.

You were born in 1968 in Sudbury, Ontario. After studying literature at Carleton University and completing an MFA at the University of New Orleans, you taught creative writing in Louisiana. Your fiction traces the entanglement of Indigenous and settler histories, the pressures of the bush and the city, and the aftershocks of war and extraction. You are known for restrained lyricism, braided narratives, and close attention to land and kinship. You divide your time between Montreal and the western James Bay coast; your second novel won the Rogers Writers’ Trust Fiction Prize.

You were born in 1970 in Cap-Haïtien, Haiti, and moved to Brooklyn as a teenager to join your parents. Educated at state schools and later earning an MFA from Columbia University, you began publishing in the mid-1990s. Your novels and stories trace families divided by dictatorship, migration, and memory, weaving Haitian oral traditions and Creole cadences into clear, restrained prose. You write as both witness and daughter, attentive to the endurance of women, the ambiguities of faith, and the costs of exile. Alongside fiction, your essays address immigration, human rights, and catastrophe at home. Your work has received a Whiting Writers’ Award and a National Book Award finalist citation.

You were born in 1932 in Brooklyn, New York. After studying literature at City College and graduate work at Columbia, you began as a reader for a film company before moving into publishing, eventually serving as an editor at Viking. Your novels braid public history with private invention, employing polyphonic narration, documentary fragments, and a cool moral intelligence to revisit American ruptures—from industrial upheaval to urban unrest—without surrendering narrative pleasure. You have taught writing at Columbia and the New School, mentoring a generation of novelists. Your work has been recognized with the National Book Critics Circle Award and the PEN/Faulkner Award, and remains central to contemporary historical fiction.

You were born in 1974 in Ottawa, Canada. After studying literature at McGill University, you lived in Chicago and Montréal, dividing your time between teaching and writing. Your early short stories appeared in Canadian and American journals before your debut novel and a subsequent collection cemented your reputation. Your work is distinguished by precise, unsentimental prose, close attention to the textures of urban youth culture, and the moral complexity of friendship and first love. Music and place are constant anchors, especially Montréal’s streets. You have taught creative writing at Concordia University and won the Journey Prize for short fiction.

You were born in 1956 in Rochester, New York. Raised in a suburb, you left home during college and lived briefly in Chicago and San Francisco before settling in New York City in the early 1980s. Supporting yourself through office work and freelance copyediting, you wrote stories and novels probing desire, power, cruelty, and the possibility of grace. Your spare, unsentimental prose, observant yet compassionate, favors ethically fraught situations, psychological scrutiny, and women whose strength is inseparable from vulnerability. To date you have published several story collections and two novels, and contributed essays to major magazines. Honors include a Guggenheim Fellowship and a PEN/Faulkner Award finalist citation.

Born in 1969 in Bristol, England, you emigrated to Canada in childhood and grew up in Toronto. Trained as a social anthropologist (BA at McGill, PhD at the London School of Economics), you turned to fiction in the late 1990s, bringing fieldwork’s attentiveness to culture, ritual, and migration. Your novels—set between East Africa, the Middle East, and Canadian cities—trace the moral lives of people navigating exile, belief, and fractured families. Critics note your lucid, lyrical prose and the quiet authority with which you render unfamiliar worlds intimate. You have taught at Canadian universities and mentored emerging writers. Your work has received major recognition, including the Rogers Writers’ Trust Fiction Prize.

You were born in 1972 in Winnipeg, Manitoba. Raised between prairie towns and the Pacific coast, you spent your twenties planting trees and supervising crews across British Columbia and Alberta before turning to writing. After study at the University of British Columbia, you published widely in Canadian journals. Your work is marked by exacting, quietly lyrical prose, unsentimental attention to labour and landscape, and an ethical curiosity about resource economies. You have won the Journey Prize and a National Magazine Award, and your debut collection brought national recognition. You divide your time between Vancouver and seasonal field work.

You were born in 1955 in Osaka, Japan. You moved to Britain in 1961, settling in Manchester. After studying philosophy at the University of Sussex, you worked in housing services before turning to fiction and screenwriting. Since the early 1980s, your English-language novels have examined memory, moral compromise, and the fragility of identity, often through restrained first-person narrators negotiating historical aftershocks. You have also written for television and collaborated with musicians. Critics note the clarity of your prose and the quiet tension beneath it. Your work has received the James Tait Black Memorial Prize and the Guardian Fiction Prize, and is widely translated.

You were born in 1958 in Harbin, China. You came of age during the Cultural Revolution, worked briefly in a state-run factory, and later served as a communications clerk in the army. After studying English literature at a provincial university, you left for the United States in 1987, completing a doctorate at Emory University and eventually teaching in Chicago. Writing in English, you depict ordinary Chinese lives and the immigrant passage with calm, incisive prose, moral clarity tempered by irony, and a steady attention to the drag of history on private desire. Your awards include the PEN/Hemingway Award and a Whiting Writers’ Award.

You were born in 1966 in Gander, Newfoundland and Labrador. Raised near the North Atlantic, you studied visual art at the Nova Scotia College of Art and Design before turning to fiction. Your early short stories appeared in Canadian journals, followed by two collections and a novel that brought national attention. You are known for lucid, sensuous prose, an exacting eye for physical detail, and narratives that probe family, labour, and risk amid maritime weather and urban edges. You have taught workshops and served as writer-in-residence in St. John’s, where you live. Your work has earned the ReLit Award for short fiction and the Thomas Head Raddall Atlantic Fiction Award.

Born in 1959 in Brighton, England, you began in community arts and adult education before committing to fiction. After several well-noted novels and story collections in the UK, you emigrated to British Columbia in the early 2000s, where you teach creative writing and contribute to radio drama. Your work is distinguished by psychological acuity, moral intelligence, and a restrained yet inventive prose style; you often trace transformations within families, institutions, and marginal communities, balancing empathy with formal precision. You have won a CBC Literary Award for short fiction and a ReLit Award for a novel, and your books are widely reviewed in Britain and Canada.

You were born in 1956 in Haifa, Israel, and moved to Montreal at the age of eight. You studied literature and linguistics at McGill and Concordia, then taught adult education and creative writing while translating from Hebrew. Your fiction, set between Israel and Canada, probes intimate relationships under political strain, uniting moral inquiry with restrained, lucid prose. You favor braided timelines, epistolary forms, and multiple viewpoints, attentive to the frictions of language, memory, and belonging. After early short stories, your novels earned national attention and a committed readership. You have received the Quebec Writers’ Federation’s Hugh MacLennan Prize for Fiction and the Canadian Jewish Book Award, and your work is widely reviewed and taught.

You were born in 1965 in Brooklyn, New York. Raised in a household of artists, you gravitated to journalism and teaching before committing to fiction. After early stories in little magazines, your first novel in the late 1990s drew attention for its exacting prose and sly formal design. A subsequent book, blending historical research with a fractured narrative voice, established you as a central figure in contemporary American metafiction. Your work is distinguished by analytic intelligence, restless structure, and a cool, mordant humor that doubts the reliability of memory and media. You teach in New York and have received a Whiting Writers’ Award and a Pushcart Prize.

You were born in 1967 in Charlottesville, Virginia. After studying English at the University of Virginia and completing an MFA at New York University, you settled in Brooklyn, balancing teaching and editing with the steady work of fiction. Your novels, noted for lucid, measured prose and a moral attentiveness to faith, desire, and community, move between historical subjects and present-day lives, often centering the private resolve of women. You have taught at Sarah Lawrence College and served on the editorial staff of Ploughshares. Your work has been recognized with a Whiting Writers’ Award and a fellowship from the National Endowment for the Arts.

Born in 1961 in San Jose, California, you studied literature and physics at a northeastern university before supporting yourself as a programmer in the Bay Area. Drawn to conflict zones and fringe economies, you reported from Afghanistan and the Balkans, turning that fieldwork into expansive novels and essays that merge documentary rigor, ethics, and lyricism. Your pages teem with footnotes, photographs, and interviews, refusing neat boundaries between fiction and reportage. You have written searchingly about prostitution, poverty, and the aftermath of war, foregrounding the voices of the overlooked. Your honors include a Guggenheim Fellowship and the National Book Critics Circle Award. You live in Oakland, California.

You were born in 1958 in Greenwood, Mississippi. Raised in a Delta farming family, you studied literature at the University of Mississippi and began publishing stories that led to a career in fiction. After early years teaching in Arkansas, you settled in Massachusetts, where you continue to write and teach. Your novels and stories probe small-town lives, racial memory, faith, and the stubborn pull of history, rendered in restrained prose and carefully layered plots. You are known for moral precision without sentimentality and for settings that bind characters to place. Your work has earned a Pushcart Prize and the Mississippi Institute of Arts and Letters Award.

You were born in 1956 in Halifax, Nova Scotia. After studying history at McGill, you worked as a journalist and later as a screenwriter in Los Angeles, before returning to fiction. Your debut novel traces North Atlantic migrations and unsettled families, joining historical sweep to intimate, salt‑weathered detail; your prose is lean, lyrical, and alert to class, faith, and the work of survival. A fellowship at the Fine Arts Work Center supported early drafts. You divide your time between Montreal and Nova Scotia’s South Shore. Your first novel received the Rogers Writers’ Trust Fiction Prize.

You were born in 1963 in Kingston, Ontario. After studying journalism at Carleton University, you built a career as a magazine writer and later a business columnist at a national newspaper, earning a reputation for rigor and clear-eyed analysis. Turning to fiction, you published two widely praised novels distinguished by sardonic humour, moral inquiry, and close observation of ambition’s costs within families and workplaces. Reviewers highlight your precise prose, restrained compassion, and sharp dialogue. You have won a National Magazine Award and the Trillium Book Award. You live in Toronto, where you continue to write and occasionally mentor emerging writers.

Born in 1967 in Walla Walla, Washington, you were raised on the Columbia Plateau and studied history at the University of Washington. After seasons as a river guide and a museum archivist, you turned to fiction, publishing a debut novel in 2005 and a second in 2009. Your books braid meticulous research with spare, lyrical prose, tracing domestic lives caught in the hazards of the nineteenth-century American West; landscape, labor, and moral ambiguity are your abiding concerns. You live near Puget Sound and occasionally teach at Seattle’s Hugo House. Your work has received the Pacific Northwest Book Award and an NEA Literature Fellowship.

Born in 1952 in Melbourne, you came to fiction through work in editing and film after studying literature at the University of Melbourne. Your novels, essays, and occasional memoir draw on archival research and family memory to interrogate Australia’s colonial past, the ethics of settlement, and the fractures of domestic life. Known for lucid, carefully wrought prose and an acute ear for voice, you fashion narratives that bridge intimate experience with public history. After years in London and New York, you now live in Sydney and teach creative writing. Your work has received the Miles Franklin Award and a NSW Premier’s Literary Award.

You were born in 1966 in Tripoli, Lebanon. As a teenager you left during the civil war, spending years in Cyprus and the United States before settling in Montreal, where you studied photography and worked as a museum archivist. Your early fiction grew from street-level observation and an immigrant’s wary eye, blending caustic wit, raw lyricism, and hallucinatory realism to portray war-haunted exiles, hustlers, and the moral ambiguities of city life. Two novels to date have brought you international notice; your debut won the Rogers Writers’ Trust Fiction Prize and the Commonwealth Writers’ Prize (Best First Book, Canada and Caribbean). You continue to write and photograph in Montreal.

You were born in 1957 in Newark, New Jersey. After studying literature and working as a journalist, you spent stretches in Moscow and Central Europe, experiences that shaped your fiction’s preoccupation with political upheaval, private duplicity, and the border between satire and tragedy. Returning to the United States, you published acclaimed short stories and novels whose precise architecture, mordant humor, and cosmopolitan intelligence made you a distinctive voice. Your work often links intimate relationships to historical convulsions, attentive to language, science, and the eccentricities of power. You have received a Guggenheim Fellowship and the O. Henry Prize.

You were born in 1975 in Ottawa, Ontario, to Chinese-Vietnamese parents. Trained at the University of Toronto, you practice emergency medicine in Toronto while writing fiction and non-fiction informed by clinical work and public health. Your early stories about medical trainees and hospitals garnered national attention for their precise observation and ethical nuance, often interweaving immigrant histories with the realities of care. During the 2003 SARS outbreak, you worked on the front lines, later contributing guidance on influenza preparedness. You have received the Rogers Writers’ Trust Fiction Prize and been shortlisted for the Scotiabank Giller Prize. You continue to balance hospital shifts with literary work.

You were born in 1969 in Rome to Libyan parents. Raised between Tripoli and Cairo, you left North Africa as a teenager and settled in London, where you studied architecture and later taught part-time while writing. The disappearance of your father under the Libyan regime shadows your work, which examines exile, filial loyalty, and the moral pressure of dictatorship through spare, lucid prose and intimate domestic scenes. Your debut novel, published in 2007, was translated into many languages, won the John Llewellyn Rhys Prize, and was longlisted for the Dylan Thomas Prize. Essays in British newspapers and journals complement your fiction.

You were born in 1958 in Oak Park, Illinois. After a childhood partly spent in Tokyo, you studied at the University of Michigan, starting in physics before turning to literature. You worked as a programmer and data analyst in Boston before publishing your first novel in the late 1980s. Your work knits together science, music, and technology through polyphonic structures, careful research, and a moral attention to connection and responsibility. Residences in Berlin and Ann Arbor shaped your perspective, and you have taught intermittently at a Midwestern university. Your books have received the National Book Critics Circle Award and a Guggenheim Fellowship.

You were born in 1970 in Quebec City. Trained in visual arts and art history, you first gained recognition as a painter before turning to fiction. In the late 1990s, you moved to Rome, later making your home in the United Kingdom, dividing your time between studio work and writing. Your novels and stories unite a painter’s attention to light and composition with reflective, carefully honed prose, exploring memory, exile, and the fragile architectures of intimate life. Widely translated, your work has earned a devoted readership. For your early books, you received the Prix Anne-Hébert and, subsequently, the Prix des libraires du Québec.

You were born in 1927 in Boston, Massachusetts. After graduating from a military academy, you flew jet fighters in the Korean War, an experience that shaped your austere, exacting sense of fate. You left the service in the late 1950s and began the slow, meticulous career of a novelist and short-story writer, dividing your years between New York and Paris, with intervals in California writing for film. Your work is distinguished by compressed, luminous prose, an unsentimental gaze on desire and class, and an almost architectural attention to scene. You have received a Guggenheim Fellowship and the American Academy of Arts and Letters Award in Literature.

Born in 1961 in Trois-Rivières, Quebec, you trained in physics and philosophy before committing to fiction and teaching. Emerging in the mid-1990s, you quickly became a distinctive voice in francophone Canadian literature: your compact, disquieting novels probe damaged families and isolated communities through baroque yet controlled prose, unreliable narrators, and a rigorous moral intelligence. You divide your time between Montreal and the Mauricie, publish essays and stories, and your work has been translated into English and several European languages, earning international readership. Honors include the Prix des libraires du Québec and the Grand Prix du livre de Montréal. Colleagues and critics alike recognize the singular architecture and austere lyricism that mark your project.

You were born in 1967 in Montclair, New Jersey. Raised in Los Angeles from adolescence, you studied film and literature at UCLA before moving to New York, where you worked in postproduction and bookstores while writing at night. You are the author of two novels from a major press, and your work is known for formally agile structures, documentary fragments, and a precise ear for the cultural noise of late‑twentieth‑century America. Your fiction probes memory, music scenes, and political idealism with skepticism and empathy. A recipient of a Whiting Writers’ Award, you live in Brooklyn and occasionally teach in the graduate writing program at NYU.

You were born in 1956 in Chicago, Illinois. After moving to Los Angeles as a teenager, you worked as a driver, location scout, and script reader before publishing fiction and writing for film and television. Your novels anatomize celebrity culture and its spiritual wreckage, blending baroque humor with moral severity and a chorus of intersecting voices. You are known for panoramic structures, prophetic monologues, and a guarded compassion for the fallen. Early acclaim led to the PEN Center USA Award for Fiction and a Guggenheim Fellowship. You live in Los Angeles, pursuing long-form projects and occasional essays.

You were born in 1966 in Tacoma, Washington. You came to fiction by way of journalism, spending a decade at a Northwest daily covering federal trials and extremist standoffs, work that honed your reportorial precision and skepticism toward official narratives. Your novels of the 2000s moved from crime‑inflected plots toward broader social satire, tracing ordinary lives through boom‑and‑bust economies, media spectacle, and political unease. Critics praise your blend of dark humor, moral clarity, and compassion for the working West, as well as your nimble shifts between suspense and intimate character study. You have been recognized with the Los Angeles Times Book Prize and the Pacific Northwest Booksellers Award.

You were born in 1968 in Swansea, Wales. Educated in English at the University of Bristol, you completed an MA at Sussex and a doctorate at the University of York on lesbian narratives in nineteenth-century popular culture. After moving to London, you lectured in literature and gender studies before turning full time to fiction in the late 1990s. Your novels, set largely in Victorian and Edwardian Britain, are distinguished by meticulous archival research, measured yet sensuous prose, and layered plots of secrecy, class tension, and desire, often centering women who resist constraint. Your work has received the Stonewall Book Award and the John Llewellyn Rhys Prize.

You were born in 1949 in Victoria, British Columbia. Raised on Vancouver Island and in the interior, you built a career as a short story writer and novelist, publishing in leading Canadian journals and releasing two collections and a novel with respected presses. After years of work in libraries and classrooms, you taught creative writing workshops and read widely across the West Coast. Your fiction is marked by luminous, economical prose, exacting attention to landscape, and quietly intricate portrayals of families in flux and the aftershocks of loss. You have won the Journey Prize and the CBC Literary Award for short fiction.

You were born in 1975 in Berkeley, California. After studying comparative literature at a state university, you worked as a reporter in the Caribbean and later in Southeast Asia, settling for several years in Chiang Mai. Your first novel, published in the late 2000s, drew on your time among missionaries and anthropologists, marrying ethnographic curiosity with the pacing of investigative narrative. Critics noted your measured prose, moral gravity, and meticulous scene-building. Essays and reportage have appeared in American magazines and Thai newspapers. You continue to divide your time between teaching, freelance journalism, and fiction. Your debut was shortlisted for the PEN/Faulkner Award and earned you a Whiting Writers’ Award.

You were born in 1971 in Vancouver, British Columbia, to parents who immigrated from Trinidad and Tobago. You grew up in East Vancouver, studied English literature at the University of British Columbia, and completed a doctorate at McGill University. You now teach contemporary literature at the University of Victoria and publish essays on diaspora and memory. Your fiction is distinguished by spare, attentive prose, intimate attention to family histories, and nuanced portrayals of race, class, and the suburbs. Your debut novel earned the Commonwealth Writers’ Prize for Best First Book (Canada and the Caribbean) and established you as a significant voice in Canadian letters.

You were born in 1960 in Portland, Oregon. Raised along the Columbia and later educated at the University of Oregon and the Iowa Writers’ Workshop, you built a career in short fiction and essays that appeared in The New Yorker, Harper’s, and The Paris Review. You have taught in Midwestern MFA programs, known for a rigorous, humane presence in the classroom. Your work dwells on damaged families, the economies of the coastal Northwest, and the moral weather of insiders turned outsiders, rendered in lucid, tensile prose. You have received a Guggenheim Fellowship and a Pushcart Prize, recognition that followed years of quiet, exacting craft.

You were born in 1949 in New Haven, Connecticut. After studying French and comparative literature at Brown, you built a life between writing and translation, teaching intermittently while publishing compact story collections and essays. Your fictions, often only a paragraph or a page, draw on ordinary domestic scenes, stray observations, and the tensions of language itself; they are marked by precision, dry wit, and an almost scientific attention to syntax and thought. Your translations from French, including work by Flaubert and Proust, have broadened your audience and deepened your style. Honors include a Guggenheim Fellowship and a Lannan Literary Award.

You were born in 1946 in Evanston, Illinois. After studying at the University of Wisconsin, you moved to New York in the early 1970s, working intermittently in theater and publishing while developing the short stories that would define your career. Your work, often first appearing in The New Yorker and similar journals, is distinguished by exacting sentences, moral intelligence, and an unflinching awareness of social and political pressures beneath ordinary life. Several collections have cemented your reputation, and you have taught for years at New York University, guiding younger writers. Honors include the Rea Award for the Short Story and a Guggenheim Fellowship. You live in Manhattan.

You were born in 1975 in Toledo, Ohio, and raised in the Midwest before studying literature at the University of Michigan, where you later earned an M.F.A. After several years as a copywriter in Chicago and New York, you turned that experience into fiction, debuting with a satirical, chorus-driven office novel that examined loyalty, fear, and the consolations of work. A second book followed, more intimate, tracing a marriage tested by an inexplicable condition. Your prose is noted for collective voice, mordant humor, and moral unease. You have received the Whiting Writers’ Award and the Los Angeles Times Art Seidenbaum Award for First Fiction.

You were born in 1953 in London, Ontario. After studying literature at the University of Western Ontario, you moved to Toronto, working as a copy editor and later an acquisitions editor while publishing reviews. Your first story collection in the late 1980s established your reputation for compassionate portraits of outsiders and for blending the uncanny with psychological detail. Subsequent novels expanded your range—from fractured families to the interior lives of animals—while maintaining moral seriousness. Your books are taught in Canadian literature courses. You have won a Commonwealth Writers' Prize for Best Book and the City of Toronto Book Award.

You were born in 1972 in Karachi and spent your childhood between Pakistan and the Gulf before leaving for the United States to study at an Ivy League university, later completing a law degree. After several years in management consulting in New York and London, you returned to Pakistan to write fiction and essays. Your novels probe globalization, class, and the uneasy traffic between commerce and conscience, often using spare prose and unconventional narration—second-person address, confessional monologue—to stage moral ambiguity. Your work has reached readers worldwide and drawn critical notice, including a shortlist for the Man Booker Prize and the Guardian First Book Award.

You were born in 1952 in Peterborough, Ontario, and came of age among lakes and long winters that later shaped your work. After university, you worked as a producer for CBC Radio in Whitehorse and Montreal, then spent several years in Mexico City and Washington, D.C., before settling in Ottawa to write full-time. Your career has moved from journalism and essays to acclaimed fiction, noted for spare, luminous prose, northern landscapes, and the intimate weather of families. Your narratives braid memory with place, the private with the public voice of radio. You have won the Rogers Writers’ Trust Fiction Prize and were a finalist for the Scotiabank Giller Prize.

You were born in 1953 in St. Louis, Missouri, and raised in coastal California. After work in journalism and a stint in workshops with Gordon Lish, you emerged as a writer of taut, elliptical short stories built on implication and silence. Your pieces—attentive to animals, illness, and the precariousness of loyalty—appear in The Paris Review, Harper’s Magazine, and Best American Short Stories. You have taught in MFA programs at the University of Michigan and Sarah Lawrence College, and you volunteer in animal rescue. A recipient of a Guggenheim Fellowship, you are known for sentences pared to necessity and a steady moral gaze that finds resonance in the smallest gesture.

You were born in 1951 in Stuttgart, Germany, the child of a diplomat, and spent your early years moving through Tokyo, Manila, and the American West. You came of age in the deserts of New Mexico, studied literature, and earned an MFA at the University of Arizona. Beginning as a poet, you went on to publish short stories, novels, and plays, as well as journalism from distant wars. Your prose is spare yet luminous, haunted by addiction, spiritual hunger, and the difficult mercy of redemption; your characters drift at society’s margins, glimpsing moments of violent clarity. You live in the Pacific Northwest, teach occasionally, and have been honored with the PEN/Faulkner Award.

You were born in 1952 in Richmond, Virginia. Raised in Washington, D.C., you held office and research jobs while writing at night. Your first collection in the early 1990s traced working-class Black neighborhoods of the capital with unsentimental tenderness and exacting detail. A later historical novel widened the canvas to the antebellum South, probing power, kinship, and conscience with panoramic clarity. You publish slowly, teach intermittently, and keep close to the mid-Atlantic streets that ground your imagination. Your prose is measured, attentive to place and moral consequence, and your communities feel fully inhabited. You have received the National Book Award and the PEN/Faulkner Award.

You were born in 1956 in Wellington, New Zealand. After studying at the University of Otago, you worked as a newspaper journalist before turning to fiction. Reporting assignments took you through Papua New Guinea, the Solomon Islands, and Fiji; those encounters inform work noted for lucid prose, moral urgency, and the mingling of history with fable. Often you write about island communities, the education of children, and the burdens of war and memory, favoring intimate narrators and a humane gaze. Your books have brought international attention, earning the Commonwealth Writers’ Prize (South East Asia and Pacific) and a shortlist for the Man Booker Prize.

Born in 1950 in Portsmouth, you spent parts of your childhood abroad as the child of a military family before studying English at the University of Bristol and completing a postgraduate degree at Lancaster University. You emerged in the mid-1970s with short stories noted for taut psychology and unsettling intimacy, then turned to novels that frame private lives within ethical and scientific dilemmas. Your prose is spare yet exacting; your narratives test responsibility, chance, and the consequences of secrecy. Alongside fiction you have written essays and screenplays and are a measured presence in public debate. Your work has earned the James Tait Black Memorial Prize and the Man Booker Prize.

Born in 1945 in Kandy, Sri Lanka, you moved to London in your teens and by the mid-1960s made Toronto your home. Trained in literature, you began as a poet before turning to fiction and essays, while teaching and editing that helped cultivate new Canadian voices. Your work is marked by lyrical intensity, shifting perspectives, and a collage of history and memory that traces migrations, intimate violence, and fragile identity. You weave archival detail with a filmmaker’s eye for scene. Your books have earned the Commonwealth Writers’ Prize and the Trillium Book Award, and your influence endures across classrooms and festivals.

You were born in 1975 in Quebec City and raised in Montreal. After studying literature at Concordia University, you supported yourself with odd jobs while writing dispatches for the Montreal Gazette and essays for The Walrus and CBC Radio. Your 2005 debut novel brought national attention, followed by a short-story collection and continued work in magazines. Your fiction is marked by lyrical, incantatory prose, child and adolescent narrators, and a compassionate, unsentimental portrait of urban poverty and fragile family bonds, often touched by a quietly surreal imagination. You have received the Amazon.ca First Novel Award and the Quebec Writers’ Federation First Book Prize.

You were born in 1934 in Elizabeth, New Jersey. Raised in a middle-class Jewish household, you studied literature at Rutgers and completed graduate work at Columbia, later teaching at Brandeis and New York University. You emerged in the early 1960s with audacious stories that scrutinized American identity and the uneasy bargains of assimilation. Over the decades, your novels, often voiced by self-questioning alter egos, braid corrosive comedy with moral seriousness, probing desire, illness, and the distortions of public scandal. Rooted in the urban Northeast yet restlessly national in scope, your work is formally agile and intellectually combative. You have received the National Book Critics Circle Award and the PEN/Faulkner Award.

You were born in 1957 in New Haven, Connecticut. After studying literature at Amherst College and earning an M.F.A. from the Iowa Writers’ Workshop, you began publishing novels and story collections on subjects from polar expeditions to nuclear testing. Your fiction is marked by meticulous research, spare, exacting sentences, and unsentimental empathy for people caught in the gears of history. Stories have appeared in Harper’s, The New Yorker, The Paris Review, and Best American Short Stories. You teach at Middlebury College, where you are known for rigorous seminars. Honors include a Guggenheim Fellowship and the Whiting Writers’ Award.

You were born in 1951 in Tanga, Tanzania, and raised in a Gujarati-speaking community. In the 1970s you left East Africa to study physics in the United States, completed a doctorate, and settled in Toronto, balancing research with the beginnings of a literary life. Since the late 1980s your novels have traced the migrations of East African Asians, the entanglements of memory and history, and the moral aftershocks of decolonization. Your prose is measured and archival, attentive to family lore and political rupture alike. You co-edited a forum for South Asian writing in Canada, and your work has earned the Rogers Writers’ Trust Fiction Prize and the Commonwealth Writers’ Prize.

You were born in 1972 in Medicine Hat, Alberta, and came of age on the Prairies before settling in Toronto. After working as a bookseller and editor, you began publishing stories in The Malahat Review, Grain, and The Fiddlehead, then moved to the novel. Your fiction is marked by lucid, tactile prose; a deep engagement with animal life and landscape; and patient, historically informed storytelling that traces fragile communities at the city’s edges. You have received the CBC Literary Award for short story and the Danuta Gleed Literary Award for your debut collection. You continue to write and teach, balancing meticulous research with an unwavering attention to compassion.

You were born in 1975 in Kochi, India. After schooling in Kerala and Mumbai, you studied economics at Columbia University and completed a master’s at Cambridge. You worked as a reporter and critic for The Economist and Time, covering business and politics across South Asia, before returning to India to write fiction. Your prose blends reportage with unsentimental social scrutiny, dark wit, and propulsive first-person narration, probing ambition, inequality, and the moral costs of rapid growth. Your debut novel, published in 2007, drew wide attention and won the Commonwealth Writers’ Prize for Best First Book in 2008.

You were born in 1964 in Santa Cruz, California. Raised in Albuquerque and coastal Maine, you studied literature at Brown University and earned an MFA from the Iowa Writers’ Workshop before settling in Brooklyn. After early work as an editor and reviewer, you built a career as a novelist and essayist, publishing urban comedies of manners distinguished by sharp psychological acuity, sensual attention to food and art, and women’s voices navigating friendship, work, and desire. Your essays have appeared in The New York Times and Food & Wine. Honors include a 2004 Whiting Writers’ Award and a 2008 Guggenheim Fellowship.

Born in 1969 in Mississauga, Ontario, you grew up between a Portuguese household and Toronto’s west-end streets. After studying literature at the University of Toronto and training as a teacher, you taught in public schools while writing fiction that maps immigrant memory onto the city’s history. Your work is marked by spare, lyrical prose, moral clarity, and close attention to working-class lives from Lisbon to Little Portugal. Early stories and a debut collection brought national attention, leading to festival invitations and translation abroad. You have worked from community archives and oral histories, and your book earned the Toronto Book Award.

You were born in 1947 in Cleveland, Ohio. After a childhood shaped by church and walks along Lake Erie, you studied English at a Virginia liberal-arts college and completed graduate work in religion. Early essays in Harper’s and The Atlantic led to books that braid field observation with metaphysical inquiry and precise, lyric prose. You have taught at small colleges and kept a modest public profile. Your work dwells on patience, the moral weight of seeing, and the strangeness of the ordinary. You have received a National Book Critics Circle Award. You now divide your time between Vermont and Washington State.

Born in 1959 in Victoria, British Columbia, you grew up between the coast and the Maritimes before settling on the Prairies. After years in theatre: acting, directing, and stage-managing, and a period producing arts features for CBC Radio, you turned to fiction. Your novels and stories examine moral responsibility within families and small communities, marrying precise observation with understated wit. Music, performance, and the rhythms of work recur in your settings, often Saskatoon and rural Saskatchewan, with forays to Atlantic Canada. You teach and serve as writer-in-residence across the West. Your work has received the Rogers Writers’ Trust Fiction Prize and the Georges Bugnet Award for Fiction.

You were born in 1957 in Cuttack, India. Trained in history at Presidency College and in anthropology at Jawaharlal Nehru University and SOAS, you moved between journalism and academia, later teaching in New York. Your fiction, written in English, fuses archival depth with lyrical clarity, tracking the entanglements of empire, migration, and commerce across the Indian Ocean. Polyphonic structures, multilingual cadences, and scrupulous attention to place distinguish your work, as do your essays on history and memory. Your books have earned international readership, and you have received the Commonwealth Writers’ Prize and the Padma Shri. You divide your time between India and the United States.

You were born in 1953 in Manchester to Jewish immigrant parents. After studying English at a redbrick university, you became a reporter for national newspapers, later a columnist and feature writer known for essays on clothes, urban life, and politics. Your novels, shaped by precise observation and a scrupulous moral intelligence, trace postwar migration, the residues of European catastrophe, and the private economies of memory; your non-fiction blends reportage with cultural history. You moved to London, dividing your time between journalism and fiction, and have read widely at festivals and taught occasional seminars. Your work has received the Costa Book Award for the Novel and the Jewish Quarterly–Wingate Prize.

You were born in 1967 in Mostar, then Yugoslavia. After arriving in New York in 1992 for a temporary program, you remained as war consumed your city, learned English quickly, and began publishing short stories and essays. Your fiction, marked by inventive language, shifting perspectives, and an ethical attention to exile, memory, and historical violence, blurs reportage and imagination while sustaining dark, unsentimental humor. Across stories and a novel, you have earned a reputation for formal daring and moral clarity. Your work has received a Whiting Writers’ Award and an NEA Literature Fellowship, and continues to appear in leading American magazines and in translation abroad.

You were born in 1964 in Reading, Berkshire. After studying English at Oxford and completing doctoral work on eighteenth-century prose, you moved from academia into journalism and fiction, becoming a regular critic for the Guardian while lecturing in creative writing at the University of East Anglia. Your novels chart the textures of British life with meticulous social observation and broad political reach, alternating between intimate domestic canvases and historically expansive narratives set beyond Britain. A clear, exacting style and architectural plotting distinguish your work. You have received the Betty Trask Award and the Encore Award.

You were born in 1969 in Seattle, Washington, and grew up on the West Coast before moving to New York. After studying comparative literature at UC Santa Cruz and cultural theory at New York University, you worked in the art world, editing and writing for publications such as Artforum and The Believer. Your fiction, grounded in rigorous research, traces the entanglement of political upheaval, avant-garde scenes, and global capital, often following women who navigate risk, velocity, and self-invention across continents. Your debut novel, published in 2009, earned the Whiting Writers’ Award and was a finalist for the PEN/Hemingway Award. You live in Brooklyn, where you continue to write criticism and fiction.

Born in 1962 in New Haven, Connecticut, you came of age on the East Coast and studied literature before emerging in the early 1980s with short stories in major magazines. Your subsequent novels and collections examine family secrecy, sexuality, and moral ambiguity with spare, exacting prose and a classical sense of structure. Moving between American suburbia and Europe, you cultivate intimate portraits of intellectual life and private longing. You have taught in university writing programs and split your time between New York and Rome. Among your honors are a Whiting Writers' Award and a Lambda Literary Award.

You were born in 1929 in Boston, Massachusetts. After college and a stint in the Navy, you drifted to Paris, where you helped launch a little magazine that drew writers across the Atlantic. Returning to the United States, you worked as a fisherman and field naturalist, then turned to books that braid reportage, travel, and a spare, meditative prose. Your journeys—from the Himalaya to the Everglades and remote coasts—frame inquiries into wilderness, justice, and the costs of ambition. A longtime Zen practitioner, you write with austere clarity and moral gravity. Your work has earned the National Book Award and the John Burroughs Medal.

You were born in 1956 in Johnson City, Tennessee, and raised in the Blue Ridge foothills. After earning degrees at East Tennessee State University and the University of North Carolina at Greensboro, you taught literature at Appalachian State University, writing across poetry, stories, and novels. Your work is distinguished by spare lyricism, historical resonance, and an unflinching gaze at the Appalachian South—its rivers and mill towns, the legacies of logging and textiles, and the stubborn bonds of family. You have been honored with an O. Henry Prize and the Thomas Wolfe Memorial Literary Award, and your books explore hard reckonings tempered by moments of hard-won grace.

You were born in 1961 in Windsor, Ontario, to Italian immigrants. After studying literature at the University of Toronto and completing graduate work in creative writing at Concordia University, you lived for periods in southern Italy, experiences that shaped your fiction. Your early novels formed a loose trilogy tracing a family's passage from a Calabrian village to urban Canada, noted for restrained prose, moral nuance, and precise attention to faith, migration, and memory. You have taught writing and taken part in PEN Canada initiatives while remaining based in Toronto. Your debut won the Governor General’s Award for Fiction, and a later book received the Rogers Writers’ Trust Fiction Prize.

You were born in 1951 in Bathurst, New Brunswick, and raised by the Nepisiguit River, where the mill’s whistle marked your early years. After a brief stay at the University of New Brunswick, you left to write full-time, publishing stories and novels that return to northern communities shaped by poverty, faith, and hard loyalty. Your prose is spare and exacting, driven by moral inquiry and a Catholic sensibility that resists sentimentality while refusing despair. You have written fiction and essays, championing those silenced by class and circumstance. Your work has received the Rogers Writers’ Trust Fiction Prize and the Thomas Head Raddall Atlantic Fiction Award.

You were born in 1976 in Erie, Pennsylvania. After studying literature at Kenyon College and earning an MFA at Columbia, you spent seasons in Sicily and the American Midwest, then settled into a rhythm of teaching and writing, with residencies at MacDowell and Yaddo. Your debut novel, published in 2008, established your reputation for choral narratives, taut sentences, and moral gravity. Your work probes immigrant neighborhoods and postindustrial shorelines, tracing the long reach of loss across families and time. Stories in Harper’s and Tin House have broadened your readership. You have been honored with a Whiting Writers’ Award and an O. Henry Prize, recognitions that affirmed a patient, exacting craft.

You were born in 1954 in Lethbridge, Alberta. After studies at the University of Alberta, you turned to documentary film and journalism, experience that grounds your fiction. Your novels trace the Canadian West through settlement and industry, attentive to the compromises of ambition, the pressures of land and weather, and family entanglements. Meticulous research, sweeping scenes, and plainspoken lyricism distinguish your style. Alongside your books, you have scripted films and mentored writers at The Banff Centre. Your work has received the Georges Bugnet Award for Fiction and the City of Calgary W.O. Mitchell Book Prize.

Born in 1961 in Kingston, Ontario, you studied history and worked as an archival researcher before turning to fiction. Your early short stories appeared in Canadian and American journals, and a novella earned you the O. Henry Prize. Your debut novel, widely praised, was shortlisted for the Governor General’s Award for Fiction. Your work is marked by precise, restrained prose, braided points of view, and a measured attention to the reverberations of war and family secrecy, often unfolding in small-town settings. You live in Ontario, where you continue to write and to mentor emerging writers.

You were born in 1974 in Melbourne, Australia. After studying literature at the University of Melbourne, you worked as a copywriter and on film crews, living for periods in Sydney, London, and New York. Your debut novel appeared in 2008 to international attention, noted for its sprawling, comic-philosophical voice, dense digressions, and an unsentimental portrait of family, ambition, and civic misrule. Your prose blends mordant humor with moral inquiry and a ceaseless curiosity about failure and fate. The book was longlisted for the Man Booker Prize and won the UTS Glenda Adams Award for New Writing. You continue to write fiction and occasional screen material between Australia and the United States.

You were born in 1935 in Leeds, and educated at Newnham College, Cambridge, then at Oxford, where you completed postgraduate work in English literature. After lecturing at a London college, you turned fully to fiction and criticism, developing an erudite prose that interlaces myth, science, and art history with attentive readings of Victorian texts. Your novels often pair scholarly inquiry with intimate narratives of desire and discovery, while your essays examine the moral reach of the imagination. Over five decades you have published widely, balancing narrative ambition with intellectual precision. Your work has been recognized with the Whitbread Novel Award and the James Tait Black Memorial Prize.

You were born in 1974 in Austin, Texas. Raised in Southern California, you studied literature at the University of California, Berkeley, and earned an MFA from the Iowa Writers’ Workshop. After early work in magazines, you turned to fiction, publishing a debut novel to wide notice and, later, a linked suite of stories. You teach creative writing at a small New England college. Your fiction draws on fairy-tale structures and classroom worlds to examine adolescence, uncertainty, and the porous boundary between imagination and ordinary life; your sentences are precise yet luminous, attentive to the quietly comic. Your honors include a Whiting Writers’ Award and a finalist citation for the PEN/Faulkner Award for Fiction.

You were born in 1964 in Grand Rapids, Michigan, and raised on a small farm where chores and riverbanks shaped your sense of place. After studying mathematics at the University of Michigan, you worked a string of practical jobs and led long-distance bicycle trips before turning to fiction, earning an MFA and settling in the lower peninsula. Your stories and novels trace the hardscrabble lives of Midwestern workers and survivors, especially women, rendered with precise physical detail, moral clarity, and unsentimental compassion. Teaching intermittently, you publish in leading journals. Your work has received a Pushcart Prize and a Whiting Writers’ Award.

You were born in 1970 in Evanston, Illinois, and raised in Texas after your family moved south. You studied literature at Harvard and completed an MFA at the University of Michigan, then worked as a researcher at Harper’s Magazine in New York before turning to fiction full-time. Across three novels, your work probes identity, secrecy, and institutional power, often situating private lives within charged political or academic settings. Your prose is exacting yet restless, favoring layered structures, shifting perspectives, and moral inquiry over easy resolution. You have received a Whiting Writers’ Award and a Guggenheim Fellowship, and you continue to teach and write in New York.

Born in 1942 in Port Elizabeth, South Africa, you studied mathematics and English before completing a doctorate in linguistics in the United States. You taught in New York and later at a university in Cape Town, then resettled in Australia in the early 2000s, where you continue to write and teach. Your fiction—spare, exacting, and morally attentive—tests authority and complicity, setting private lives against historical pressure. Autobiographical narratives and essays probe language, cruelty, and the claims of conscience, with a sustained concern for animals and the limits of empathy. Your work has earned major recognition, including the Neustadt International Prize for Literature.

You were born in 1967 in Grand Falls-Windsor, Newfoundland and Labrador. Raised on the northeast coast, you studied English at Memorial University and completed graduate work at Dalhousie before turning to writing full time. You began with poetry and short fiction rooted in outport life and Labrador histories, then moved to novels in the mid-2000s. Your work is marked by austere, lyrical prose, an exacting sense of place, and narratives that braid folklore with archival fact, tracing communities pressed by weather, faith, and trade. You teach across Atlantic Canada. Your books have received the Atlantic Poetry Prize and the Thomas Head Raddall Atlantic Fiction Prize.

You were born in 1957 in Kingston, Ontario. After studies in comparative literature at McGill and a doctorate on oral storytelling at the University of British Columbia, you worked as a producer at CBC Radio and taught creative writing at Concordia. Your novels trace the crossings of love and history, marrying lyrical, economical prose with myth, music, and testimony. Fieldwork in Southeast Asia and the Balkans informs your portraits of political violence and its aftermath, while your translations and essays extend this conversation beyond fiction. You have received the Toronto Book Award and a CBC Literary Award, and your work is widely translated.

You were born in 1975 in Guildford, Surrey. After reading English at Cambridge, you completed a writing degree at Royal Holloway and began a career that moves between fiction and narrative poetry. Your early novel introduced your fascination with unsettled minds and unlikely communities; a subsequent long poem, set amid colonial turmoil, refined your austere lyricism and moral intensity. A later historical novel drew wide acclaim for its precise evocation of landscape and the inner weather of its characters. You are known for compressed, musical prose, careful research, and empathy without sentimentality. Your work has been recognized with the Somerset Maugham Award.

You were born in 1972 in Kingston, Ontario, and grew up on the Pacific coast. After studying philosophy and music at the University of British Columbia, you turned to writing, publishing short fiction and essays before a breakout historical novel set in classical Greece. Your work is distinguished by economical prose, intellectual rigor, and a precise dramatization of mentorship, power, and moral choice, grounded in meticulous research. You teach and mentor emerging writers while continuing to contribute to Canadian journals. Your debut earned the Ethel Wilson Fiction Prize and the Commonwealth Writers’ Prize (Canada and Caribbean) for Best First Book, alongside shortlistings for major national honours.

You were born in 1944 in Bonavista, Newfoundland and Labrador. Raised in a coastal Catholic household and later in Cape Breton, you built a career in journalism before turning to fiction. After reporting for regional newspapers and CBC Radio, you became a familiar presence on national television, hosting a leading investigative current affairs program. Your fiction draws on Atlantic communities shaped by migration, labour, and the church, marked by spare, precise prose and moral inquiry sharpened by reporting. You balance skepticism with compassion, mapping the costs of secrecy and loyalty. Your work has earned the Rogers Writers’ Trust Fiction Prize and a Gemini Award, and you continue to write and report from Toronto and Nova Scotia.

You were born in 1953 in Stockport, England. Raised in a Catholic household, you studied history at the University of Manchester before working in a legal aid office and, later, as a literary critic. Years spent in Nigeria and Kuwait sharpened your sense of power, exile, and the fragility of social order. Your novels move between the contemporary and the rigorously reimagined past, favoring chambers over battlefields and the morally charged interiority of statesmen and strivers. An extended illness refined your attention to the body and will. A revisionist Tudor novel brought wide recognition, followed by essays and stories for national journals. Your honors include the James Tait Black Memorial Prize and the Somerset Maugham Award.

You were born in 1951 in Manchester, England. After studying biochemistry at the University of Cambridge, you taught biology in British and international schools, later spending long periods in Italy and Central Europe. Your fiction fuses genetics with twentieth-century history, noted for lucid, restrained prose, architectural motifs, and an unsentimental concern with moral choice, exile, and memory. You have published acclaimed novels and short stories and lecture on literature and science. Your work has been recognized with the McKitterick Prize and the James Tait Black Memorial Prize. You now divide your time between Rome and Prague, continuing to write.

You were born in 1972 in Singapore to Canadian parents and spent your childhood in Europe and the Caribbean before settling in Canada. You studied literature at Queen’s University and completed graduate research at the University of Oxford, then worked in publishing while developing your first novel. A second book followed in 2009. Your fiction probes desire, class, and the tensions of institutional life, often through inventive points of view and exacting, musical prose. Based in Ottawa, you examine public and private power with restraint and moral clarity. Your work has earned the Ottawa Book Award and the Rogers Writers’ Trust Fiction Prize.

You were born in 1966 in Cork, Ireland. You began as a young reporter for a national daily, then spent years traveling across Europe and the United States before settling in New York City in the mid-1990s. Your fiction, noted for lyrical compression and polyphonic structure, interlaces ordinary lives with public history, moving between Ireland, America, and Eastern Europe. You are drawn to voices at the margins and to the quiet hinge-moments that change a city’s weather. Several novels and story collections have secured international readership; you lecture widely and teach creative writing in New York. Honors include the PEN/Faulkner Award and the Rooney Prize for Irish Literature.

You were born in 1960 in Montreal, Quebec. Raised between languages and histories, you began as a poet in the 1980s, publishing widely and teaching creative writing at the University of Toronto. Your transition to fiction brought a first novel in the late 1990s and a second a decade later, each marked by painstaking research and a lyric attention to memory, exile, and the moral weight of history. Your sentences carry a poet’s compression; images return like recurring motifs in music. Landscape, architecture, and science anchor private grief. You have received the Griffin Poetry Prize and the Scotiabank Giller Prize, and your work is taught across Canada and abroad.

You were born in 1964 in Boston, Massachusetts, to a Pakistani father and an American mother, and spent childhood years between Lahore and a family farm in southern Punjab. Educated at Princeton and Harvard Law, you worked as a corporate lawyer in New York before returning to Pakistan to manage orchards and write. Your fiction, often set amid landowners, servants, and lawyers, is marked by spare, patient prose and an unsentimental eye for patronage and class, linking private fates to rural economies. Stories have appeared in the New Yorker and Granta, and your 2009 debut collection drew international notice. You have received a Whiting Writers’ Award and an O. Henry Prize.

You were born in 1932 in Goderich, Ontario. After studying English at the University of Toronto, you left to marry and moved to Vancouver, British Columbia, working in a bookshop while raising a family. Returning later to southwestern Ontario, you built a career in short fiction, publishing in Canadian magazines and The New Yorker. Your stories, set largely in small towns and farm country, are marked by lucid understatement, shifting timelines, and an exacting moral intelligence, particularly in depicting the inner lives of women and the residue of memory. You have received the Scotiabank Giller Prize and remain devoted to the short story form.

You were born in 1966 in Galway, Ireland, to an Irish father and Turkish mother. Raised in Istanbul and The Hague, you studied law at Oxford and practiced as a barrister in London before relocating to New York. Your fiction and nonfiction follow migration, family history, and post-9/11 urban life; attentive to class and sport—especially football—as social grammar, your prose marries forensic clarity to lyrical restraint. After early novels and a memoir, a breakout work drew wide notice and won the James Tait Black Memorial Prize and the Kerry Group Irish Novel of the Year. You teach and publish essays in journals.

You were born in 1951 in Jersey City, New Jersey. Raised in working‑class neighborhoods, you studied sociology at Rutgers before earning an MFA at New York University. Your early novels brought you rapid attention for unsentimental portraits of urban life, and your career expanded to screenwriting and consulting on acclaimed crime dramas for film and cable television. Your work is distinguished by exacting reportage, morally ambivalent characters, and dialogue that captures the cadences of Northeastern streets without resorting to caricature. You have taught occasional workshops, but your focus remains long-form fiction rooted in contemporary cities. Your honors include an Edgar Award and a Guggenheim Fellowship. You live in New York City.

You were born in 1962 in Vancouver, British Columbia. After relocating to London in the late 1980s, you built a career as a novelist and short-story writer while pioneering digital fiction that merges text, sound, and image. Your work often examines migration, intimacy, and class, moving between historical settings and contemporary urban life with restrained prose and careful attention to voice. You have taught creative writing at the University of East Anglia and collaborated with artists and programmers on networked narratives. Your books and digital projects have earned wide recognition, including the Commonwealth Writers’ Prize (Canada and the Caribbean) for Best Book.

You were born in 1968 in Missoula, Montana, and grew up on the Flathead Reservation. A member of the Confederated Salish and Kootenai Tribes, you left to attend the University of Montana, later settling in Portland. Beginning as a poet, you expanded into short fiction and novels, bringing comic bite and moral gravity to stories that traverse reservation roadways and city streets. Your work is distinguished by rapid-fire dialogue, tender scrutiny of family bonds, and an unflinching view of history’s burdens on contemporary Native life. Widely taught and performed, you have received a Whiting Writers’ Award and been a PEN/Hemingway finalist.

You were born in 1944 in Dauphin, Manitoba, to a Mennonite mother and a Métis father. After years in Winnipeg and Regina, you turned from clerical and advertising work to fiction, building a career from short stories to acclaimed novels that map Prairie histories and the fractures of migration. Your prose is unsentimental yet lyrical, attentive to weather, memory, and the tenuous bonds of kin. You braid Mennonite remembrances with the public record—pogroms, displacement, floods—without sacrificing intimate character studies. Widely taught, you have mentored emerging writers across the Prairies. Your honors include the Marian Engel Award and the McNally Robinson Book of the Year.

You were born in 1946 in Ballarat, Victoria. After early work in advertising in Melbourne, you began publishing short fiction and moved into novels that reimagined Australia’s colonial past with exuberant wit and moral gravity. A period in London preceded your relocation to New York in the early 1990s, where you continue to write and teach in a graduate writing program. Your books are distinguished by agile, inventive structures, a satiric edge toward authority, and a voice that fuses vernacular energy with high-art play. Your international reputation rests on major prizes, including the Booker Prize and the Commonwealth Writers’ Prize.

Born in 1970 in Cork, Ireland, you left for graduate study in English at Oxford before settling in Montréal in the late 1990s. Since your early twenties you have built a dual career as novelist and playwright, publishing fiction noted for rigorous historical research and for contemporary stories that probe family bonds, secrecy, and power. Your trademark is the charged intimacy of confined settings, rendered in precise, compassionate prose and grounded in meticulous archival work. Alongside essays and radio drama, your novels have earned a devoted readership and critical recognition, including the Stonewall Book Award and a Lambda Literary Award.

You were born in 1965 in Port Elizabeth, South Africa. Raised amid the last years of apartheid, you studied drama at the University of the Witwatersrand before turning to fiction and occasional playwriting. Publishing your first novel in your early twenties, you have since built a steady body of work marked by austere, lucid prose, moral unease, and the quiet pressure of history on intimate lives. Your narratives often trace travellers and exiles through South African landscapes and farther afield, attentive to shifting loyalties and the failures of empathy. Your fiction has received the Sunday Times Fiction Prize and the M-Net Literary Award.

Born in 1945 in Washington, D.C., you came of age amid the ferment of postwar American letters. After a B.A. at Bard College and an M.A. at Johns Hopkins University, you built a career that paired demanding, language-driven novels with devoted teaching at Wayne State University. Your work, emerging in the 1970s and maturing across subsequent decades, is marked by baroque sentences, dark wit, and a compassionate gaze toward shabby, working-class worlds—carnivals, backstretch towns, and other provisional communities. You return obsessively to risk, desire, and stubborn dignity. Your honors include a National Endowment for the Arts Literature Fellowship and a Pushcart Prize.

You were born in 1965 in Wikwemikong, Ontario. Raised in an Anishinaabe community, you developed a voice that merges sharp wit with measured social critique. After studying theatre and English in Toronto, you worked as a playwright, essayist, and novelist, writing for stage, television, and print while mentoring emerging Indigenous artists. Your work foregrounds contemporary First Nations life, cross-cultural encounter, and the tensions between community tradition and urban modernity, often using humor to reveal complex ethics. Your plays have toured nationally, your fiction is taught in universities, and you have received a Dora Mavor Moore Award and the Chalmers Canadian Play Award.

You were born in 1943 in Leeds, raised in a Jewish household attentive to comedy and argument. After reading English at Oxford and teaching in Australia and the Midlands, you settled in London as a novelist, essayist, and broadcaster. Your work fuses erudite wit with moral inquiry, anatomising desire, embarrassment, and the burdens of identity, and often satirises academic and media pretensions. Your prose is exacting, aphoristic, and steeped in literary history. Beyond fiction, you contribute a regular column to the Guardian and publish criticism. Among honours, you have won the Bollinger Everyman Wodehouse Prize and the James Tait Black Memorial Prize.

You were born in 1957 in Roanoke, Virginia. Raised in the Blue Ridge, you trained as a biologist before turning to journalism and fiction. Field seasons in Mexico and the American Southwest sharpened your focus on ecological interdependence and social justice. Your novels and essays braid scientific clarity with intimate, multi-voiced storytelling, attentive to working-class lives, migration, land stewardship, and resilient communities. You have written widely for national magazines and championed local food and public literacy. Settled in northern New Mexico, you continue to teach, lecture, and publish across genres. Your work has been recognized with the Dayton Literary Peace Prize and a PEN Center USA Award.

Born in 1976 in Brooklyn, New York, you grew up in a Jewish household and studied literature at Columbia before a Fulbright year in London. You began as a poet, then turned to novels that braid voices, letters, and memory. Your debut appeared in 2003; a second novel in 2006 broadened your audience, and a recent work deepens your preoccupations with diaspora, inheritance, and postwar history. Your fiction is noted for moral seriousness, formal elegance, and attention to how private lives intersect with events. You have received the Whiting Writers’ Award and the Rona Jaffe Foundation Writers’ Award, and you live in Brooklyn.

You were born in 1958 in Hackney, London, to parents who migrated from Barbados in the post-war years. After studying graphic design and working in community arts, you began writing in your thirties. Your novels and stories chart the crossings between the Caribbean and Britain, attentive to class, race, and the legacies of empire. You favor polyphonic structures, measured wit, and close social detail, giving voice to ordinary lives. Earlier books traced second-generation experience in late-20th-century London; more recent work turns to 19th-century plantation history and its aftermath. You have received the Commonwealth Writers’ Prize for Best Book, and your work is widely taught.

Born in 1973 in Antigonish, Nova Scotia, you came of age on the Atlantic coast before studying literature at St. Francis Xavier and McGill, and completing graduate work at the University of Toronto. You now teach in Halifax, balancing scholarship with fiction that has appeared in leading Canadian journals. Your stories are marked by meticulous structure, clear-eyed moral attention, and an unsentimental focus on labour, family, and the body under pressure, often set between the Maritimes and industrial southern Ontario. A debut collection from a Canadian press has earned wide notice. Your work has been recognized with the Journey Prize and a National Magazine Award.

You were born in 1971 in Bristol, England. After reading English and philosophy at Cambridge, you settled in London, working in community radio and collaborating with artists on installations. Your fiction and criticism probe systems of communication, accident, and memory, fusing archival research with rigorous formal design. Technical vocabularies of engineering, finance, and telecommunications thread through your sentences, which favor recursion and precise cadence over confession. You have translated contemporary French theory and curated symposia linking literature to media archaeology. Your work has appeared in journals and galleries, and an early novel earned the Somerset Maugham Award, confirming your reputation in Britain’s experimental prose.

You were born in 1958 in Rochester, New York. After earning a B.A. at SUNY Geneseo and an M.F.A. at Syracuse, you built a career in short fiction and the novel, publishing in The New Yorker, Harper’s, and other journals. Since the late 1980s you have taught at the University of Minnesota, where your workshops are exacting and generous. Your stories braid mordant humor with lyric precision, wordplay with moral restlessness, tracing the bruised comedy of love, family, and American solitude. You have received a Whiting Writers’ Award and a Guggenheim Fellowship, and your work remains a touchstone for younger writers and attentive readers.

You were born in 1975 in Sudbury, Ontario. After studying English at Queen’s University and attending the Banff Centre’s Writing Studio, you settled in Toronto, where you teach and write. Your short fiction has appeared in The Walrus and The Malahat Review, noted for clear, exacting prose, measured humor, and close observation of friendship, class, and the rituals of everyday life. Your debut collection has brought national notice. Honors include being a finalist for the Journey Prize and longlisted for the Scotiabank Giller Prize. Your work is marked by restraint, moral nuance, and the quiet intensities of ordinary moments.

You were born in 1958 in Raleigh, North Carolina. After studying literature, you left the United States, spending long stretches in Dublin and Nairobi before making a home in London. Your novels probe uneasy domestic bonds and the unintended consequences of choice, often through coolly unsentimental narrators and meticulous social observation. A breakthrough book about parental ambivalence and violence brought a wide readership, cementing your reputation for moral rigor and provocation. You have published both journalism and fiction, favoring exacting prose over sentiment. For one of these novels, you received the Costa Novel Award.

You were born in 1981 in Halifax, Nova Scotia. You grew up along the Atlantic coast, studied English at Dalhousie and completed an MA at Concordia before working in Montreal and the United States as a teacher and editor. Beginning with two slim collections of poetry and a debut novel from a small Canadian press, your work is marked by lucid, lyrical prose, an ethic of attentiveness, and sustained inquiries into memory, intergenerational debt, and the legacies of war. You have read widely across Canada and abroad. Your fiction has been shortlisted for the Scotiabank Giller Prize, and your poetry received a CBC Literary Award.

You were born in 1953 in Saskatoon, Saskatchewan. Raised on the prairie, you studied English at the University of Saskatchewan and remained in the province, combining editorial work and community arts with a steady practice of fiction. Beginning with short stories and later turning to novels, your writing is marked by spare, unsentimental prose, quiet humor and patient attention to the ties between land and family in small Western communities. Critics note your talent for interwoven narratives and the dignity you grant ordinary lives. You have received a Saskatchewan Book Award and were shortlisted for the Governor General’s Literary Award for fiction.

You were born in 1956 in Gulfport, Mississippi. Raised along the Gulf Coast, you worked as a reporter before completing an MFA at the University of Alabama. Your debut story collection in the mid-1990s drew national attention, and a subsequent novel deepened your reputation for lyrical, meticulously observed prose rooted in small-town lives and the tidal pull of memory, grief, and stubborn desire. Your work blends dark humor with a patient moral clarity, attentive to the weather and history of the Deep South. You have taught at the University of Mississippi and later in a western program. Honors include a Whiting Award and an O. Henry Prize.

You were born in 1971 in Newark, New Jersey. After studying literature at Princeton University, you worked as a researcher and book critic in Manhattan before turning to fiction. Your novels and essays explore how American history, technology, and urban space shape identity, often using speculative frameworks to recast familiar narratives. With exacting prose and understated wit, you balance structural invention with humane observation. Your work appears in national magazines and you have taught writing at Columbia and at summer workshops. Honors include a Guggenheim Fellowship and the New York Public Library Young Lions Fiction Award. You live in Brooklyn, continuing to draft ambitious, intellectually searching books.

Born in 1962 in Halifax, Nova Scotia, you grew up on Newfoundland’s coast before making homes in St. John’s and Montreal. After years as a columnist and CBC producer, you turned to fiction; your short stories earned the Metcalf-Rooke Award, and your recent debut novel has drawn national praise. Your work is marked by lyrical precision, compassionate portraits of outport life, and a probing engagement with gender, belonging, and the North’s austere beauty. You balance journalism with literary mentorship.
